Remember one sentence: outpatient doctors solve the problem of "how to admit patients", while resident doctors solve the problem of "how to pass every test after admission" - every change in the patient in the middle of the night is focused on you.

This role does not suit people who avoid responsibility, cannot tolerate night shifts, or struggle to communicate. Hospitalists carry direct responsibility for patient care. Missing an indicator could have serious consequences, and poor communication can quickly create conflict with families.

The common paths are: undergraduate degree in clinical medicine → regular training (standardized training for residents) → pass the practicing physician examination → accumulate inpatient experience in internal medicine/general medicine → become a full-time resident → upgrade to a subspecialty, attending physician or hospital management.

This role suits logical, resilient communicators who can stay focused through long shifts. Hospitalists must identify clinical priorities quickly, handle overnight emergencies independently, and explain difficult decisions with both expertise and empathy.

Hospitalists are physicians who are responsible for the diagnosis and treatment of inpatients. They manage the entire medical diagnosis and treatment of patients during their stay in the hospital, from admission assessment, daily ward rounds, treatment plan formulation and adjustment, to discharge guidance and in-hospital coordination.

Write medical orders, order examinations and tests, and interpret results.
Organize or participate in consultations, coordinate department transfers, and connect inside and outside the hospital.
Communicate the condition with patients and their families and sign informed consent.
Write medical records, course records and discharge summaries.

paragraphs: The day begins with a morning meeting and shift handoff. Every patient is reviewed during rounds, while new admissions require histories, physical examinations, and test orders. Afternoons bring test results and care discussions, sometimes with questions from three families at once. Night shifts demand independent decisions about changing conditions, emergency transfers, and critical care.

In one sentence: admission and assessment, ward rounds and prescription of medicines, checking examination results, discussing the condition, and writing medical records. Specifically, it includes admission processing, daily ward rounds, treatment decision-making, consultation coordination, family communication, medical records and discharge management.

In terms of direction, the aging of the population and the increase in chronic diseases are driving demand for hospitalization, and resident physicians are expanding as full-time positions; AI will reduce the burden of paperwork but will not replace clinical decision-making. Data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) show that there will be approximately 340,700 resident physicians on the job in 2024, and the number is expected to rise to 349,300 by 2034, with a net increase of approximately 8,600 positions, an average of approximately 9,600 vacancies per year, and a median annual salary of ≥$239,200 in 2024 (BLS OES Top Grade, 2026).

It can accelerate documentation, order entry, preliminary image review, and literature searches, leaving physicians more time for rounds and communication. Diagnosis, treatment choices, assessment of disease progression, and patient trust remain human responsibilities.

paragraphs: A 6/10, moderate AI exposure score reflects extensive automation of documentation and retrieval. Core responsibilities such as rounds, diagnosis, treatment decisions, and communication still require a physician's judgment.

Medium and high exposure does not mean high risk: AI can help doctors relieve the burden of paperwork, but it is an opportunity for the industry to "reduce" the burden. What we really need to be wary of is the inert thinking that treats AI results as conclusions; treating AI as a second opinion and an efficiency tool, clinical judgment and communication skills are still irreplaceable moats.

To study medicine, one must be mentally prepared for "long investment and slow return": undergraduate studies plus regular training should start at least eight years ago. Think clearly about whether you can withstand high intensity and night shifts; studying medicine in the AI ​​era requires more attention to clinical thinking and communication training. These are core abilities beyond examinations.

Use AI tools to reduce the paperwork burden and spend time on difficult cases and communication between doctors and patients. By delving deeper into subspecialties (critical care, cardiology, respiratory, etc.), the composite value of resident physicians will become higher and higher.

It is basically impossible to transfer non-clinical majors to residents, but medical assistance, nursing, and medical informatization can cut into the clinical ecology. Those with a nursing or medical technology background can first work in department coordination or medical record management positions.

The main reasons for the loss of resident doctors are intensity and burnout. It is recommended to use "reasonable scheduling + information-based burden reduction + professional title channel" to retain them. When purchasing AI tools, priority should be given to those that can reduce paperwork and return doctors’ time to patients.

This profession is suitable for people who "have a mission to save people and can withstand heavy pressures" - during ward rounds, they see patients getting better day by day, and their families go from anxious to relieved. This professional value of being trusted and needed is a long-term reward beyond money.

The most fulfilling thing in this profession is "bringing a serious patient back from danger" - the eyes of family members are full of anxiety when he is admitted to hospital, and the patient can walk away on his own when discharged. This kind of visible treatment result is the most direct career reward for residents.

subject.summary: Resident doctors are "the full housekeepers of patients during their hospitalization" - outpatient doctors are responsible for "taking in", and resident doctors are responsible for "safety of stay and clear treatment". The status of patients when they are discharged is the result of their benchmarking.
